transcript.reader:
Two questions to start.

1. This document answers more than one question, so let me freeze one before I test anything. Is the claim you want tested (a) "each CONSORT item earns its place, because a report without it cannot be appraised and the trial methods it describes are tied to biased estimates," or (b) "the 2010 revision was the right response to what had accumulated since 2001"? Which of those is central, and over what range does it hold — two-group parallel drug trials only, or every report that calls itself a randomised trial?

2. Take one item, 8a, the method used to generate the allocation sequence. If I cut that item out of the checklist and leave everything else, what can a reader no longer do, and where in a real report would we see the difference? Now give me the other half of the same poke: what change to how sequence generation is described in a report should make no difference at all?
transcript.author:
**1.** The central claim is (a), but in a weaker form than you've stated it. What I defend is the reporting claim: without a description of design, conduct, and analysis, readers cannot appraise a trial — plus the narrower empirical claim that a few specific features (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, selective outcome reporting) are associated with biased estimates. I do *not* claim every item maps onto bias. The document says CONSORT "was not meant to be used as a quality assessment instrument"; items on eligibility, settings, and generalisability address external validity, and I explicitly note that much worth reporting — ethics approval, informed consent, data monitoring — sits outside the checklist. So "each item earns its place because its methods are tied to biased estimates" overstates my evidence.

Claim (b) is a defensible judgment, not a testable proposition, and I'd defend it narrowly: the revision responded to genuinely new evidence — protocol–publication discrepancies, selective outcome reporting — not to proof that revising improved anything.

Scope: aimed at primary reports of two-group parallel trials; most of it is relevant to factorial, cluster, crossover, and non-inferiority designs, but those need their published extensions. Not every report calling itself randomised — some are not randomised at all, which is precisely why item 8a matters.

**2.** Cut 8a and a reader can no longer distinguish an unpredictable chance-based sequence from a deterministic one. "Randomised" alone is uninformative — readers "cannot judge adequacy from such terms as random allocation, randomisation, or random" without elaboration. Alternation, hospital numbers, or date of birth get called random routinely. Without the mechanism you cannot code selection-bias risk, cannot tell whether the sequence could be anticipated or reconstructed (which matters even when concealment is described), and cannot feed the trial into methodological reviews or sensitivity analyses. It shows up right where the evidence is: 21% of PubMed-indexed trials in 2000 and 34% in 2006 reported an adequate generation method, so most reports were unclassifiable. "Patients were randomised" versus "computer-generated list, stratified by centre, permuted blocks of 2, 4, and 6" is the difference between unclear and low risk.

Conversely, changes carrying no new information should make no difference: naming the software package (Stata vs SAS vs R), reporting the seed, or rephrasing the same mechanism in synonyms. The item asks about unpredictability, not brand. Dropping a random element — pure minimisation — is different, and does matter.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

3. You've split the checklist in two: items where you have a measured link to bias (sequence generation, concealment, blinding, selective outcome reporting), and items held only by "readers cannot appraise" (eligibility, settings, dates, design type). For one of the second kind — take 4b, settings and locations — name a change to the world that should alter what a reader concludes if that item is really doing that work, and one change that should not. Then: what reading would tell you an item has been put in the wrong group, and where would you go looking for it?

4. You write that "the introduction of CONSORT within journals is associated with improved quality of reports." Which study is that, comparing what with what? And if reporting quality in journals that never adopted CONSORT improved over the same years, what in your explanation stays put — and what would you have to give up?
transcript.author:
**3.** Item 4b does external-validity work, so it earns its place only if applicability judgments move when the world moves. Two cases:

*Should matter.* The reader's setting diverges from the trial's in ways that plausibly shift baseline risk, resources, or standard care. The Blantyre example — one antiretroviral clinic, 27% adult HIV prevalence — transports differently to a setting with different prevalence and treatment access. So does a change in the world after publication: if a trial site later gains or loses access to the standard of care, the old setting description changes what a reader should conclude about applying the result. Single- versus multicentre status is the same kind of information.

*Should not matter.* Cosmetic description: "Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Blantyre, Malawi" versus the same content split across two sentences, sites listed in a table rather than prose, or the city name translated. Same content, same inference.

*Wrong group?* If variation in an item tracks something beyond reporting — if effect estimates differ by multicentre status or eligibility restrictiveness after adjusting for other items — then 4a/4b belong with the bias items. If setting descriptions never move readers' applicability judgments, the item is ornamental. Where I'd look: protocol–publication discrepancy reviews, meta-epidemiological studies, the transportability literature, and empirical tests of reader inference. And I'd watch confounding — the document itself notes ITT reporting co-occurs with other good practices, so a lone item may just mark overall care.

**4.** The sentence appears without a citation, and that is a defect I should own. The closest documented comparison in the document is not about adopting journals in general: in a review of 403 RCTs in 10 leading medical journals in 2002, 62% reported ITT for the primary analysis, and this was higher in journals adhering to CONSORT — 70% versus 48%. That is cross-sectional, one item, and does not isolate CONSORT. Separately, a 1998 review of five general and internal medicine journals found reporting more thorough when a flow diagram was included — observational again. I cannot point you to a randomised or interrupted-time-series evaluation from this document, and I should not pretend the general claim rests on one.

If non-adopting journals improved over the same years, the secular trend kills the causal reading. What stays: everything not dependent on CONSORT's effect — reporting is measurably incomplete; inadequate concealment, unblinded assessment, and selective outcome reporting accompany larger effect estimates; the checklist specifies what a reader needs; and CONSORT is explicitly not a quality-assessment instrument. What goes: "the introduction of CONSORT… is associated with improved quality" as evidence of efficacy. I'd downgrade it to "quality improved over this period, and CONSORT-adopting journals report better on some items, for reasons inseparable from journal selection." The tool then survives on content validity, not demonstrated effect.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

5. On 11a: you say blinding of data collectors is "unlikely to matter for objective outcomes, such as death" but matters for subjective ones. Give me the change to a trial that should move the result through blinding, and the change that should not. Then keep hold of the same part through both: is the item about the blinding itself, or about the description of the blinding? If a well-blinded trial reports only the words "double blind," is the reader worse off under your item — and what observation would show that?

6. Two parts changed between versions. You dropped the call for "intention-to-treat" analysis in favour of describing exactly who was included, because 13% of trials claiming ITT had excluded patients. And you cut the advice to test whether blinding held, because a participant who knows the outcome answers differently. For each: same claim as before, or a new one — and what does the new wording now have to account for that the old wording did not?
transcript.author:
**5.** *Should move it.* Same trial, same intervention, but the outcome assessors or data collectors know allocation and the endpoint is subjective — pain, PASI, a functional score. Differential assessment, differential encouragement, repeat measurement of abnormal findings. Swapping the outcome from all-cause death to an assessor-rated symptom is the cleanest version: blinding now has a channel to act through. *Should not move it.* Relabelling: the same people blinded, described as "double blind" rather than "participants and outcome assessors blinded." Nobody's blinding status changed, so the estimate shouldn't; only the reader's ability to classify the trial does.

Holding that part through both: item 11a's target is the blinding actually done — *who* was blinded — with the description as the vehicle. It is a reporting item about a trial feature. So yes, a well-blinded trial reporting only "double blind" leaves the reader worse off: the trial is fine, the item is failed. The document's evidence is that 200 RCTs reported as double blind yielded 18 different combinations of groups actually blinded, and about one in five did not blind participants, providers, or data collectors. The observation that would show the reader is worse off: assessors cannot reliably code "double blind" reports for whether outcome assessors were blinded, and their performance/detection-bias judgments diverge. If "double blind" reliably implied blinded outcome assessment, the item would be redundant for those trials.

**6.** Both are new claims, and both narrow what CONSORT asserts.

*ITT.* The old text endorsed a strategy — analyse as randomised. Revised item 16 is a description requirement: for each group, the number included in each analysis and whether analysis was by original assigned groups. The shift follows evidence that the label is unreliable: of 119 reports claiming ITT, 15 excluded patients; among 403 RCTs, 62% reported ITT but only 39% of those actually analysed all participants as randomised, over 60% having missing primary-outcome data. The new wording must account for what the label concealed — denominators per analysis, consistency with the flow diagram, and how missing outcomes were handled. It must also allow that strict ITT is often unachievable. I gave up prescribing a method; I kept the demand that readers can reconstruct who was analysed.

*Blinding tests.* The old advice treated asking participants as evidence about blinding. The new text calls that uninterpretable: participants usually know whether they had the outcome, so answers may reflect accurate inference about efficacy, not broken blinding. The new wording must account for that confound and substitutes two things — similarity of interventions (11b) as evidence of method, and reporting of any known unblinding. The cost is real: I now ask for less information about blinding, deliberately, because what I asked for was misleading.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

7. You name two pairs that pull against each other. Blocking buys balance in group sizes and costs unpredictability of the sequence — your own words. Minimisation buys balance on chosen characteristics, and you say it "lacks the theoretical basis for eliminating bias on all known and unknown factors" while noting that some argue it is superior. For each pair: which one gives way, and where is the line drawn? Then, what measurement would show the line is in the wrong place — for minimisation, what would you need to see in trials that used it to move the line, and what would you need to see to move it back?

8. Two limits were set before the test: the checklist is aimed at two-group parallel trials, with other designs handled by separate extensions; and "any other aspects of a trial that are mentioned should be properly reported." Take the second first — is that the same claim as the checklist, or a new one, and what would we measure to see whether it is swallowing a job the checklist ought to be doing? Then the first: swap "two-group parallel" for crossover or cluster — what breaks, and can you show me the place in the document that carries the reason for drawing the limit there?
transcript.author:
**7.** *Blocking.* Unpredictability is what gives way — but not silently. The line: you may buy balance by restriction provided the residual predictability is disclosed and mitigated. The document's remedy is "blinding the interventions, using larger block sizes, and randomly varying the block size"; item 8b then requires block size, whether fixed or varied, and disclosure if trialists became aware of it, since that knowledge permits code breaking. Stratification inherits the cost: "stratification without blocking is ineffective," so it cannot circumvent restriction. The price is paid in disclosure, not in unmeasured risk.

*Minimisation.* Here the theoretical guarantee gives way. Minimisation "lacks the theoretical basis for eliminating bias on all known and unknown factors," yet is "considered methodologically equivalent to randomised trials, even when a random element is not incorporated." That is a real concession, and it rests on argument, not measurement — I should say so. A random component is preferred. Item 8b requires naming the scheme and variables.

What would move the line? Toward scepticism: evidence that minimised allocations are computable — someone knowing the algorithm and the current imbalance can derive the next assignment — or meta-epidemiological evidence of larger effects than randomised trials at comparable concealment. Toward the current position: comparable effect estimates, balanced unmeasured prognostic factors in simulation, and documented concealment. I cannot point to either in this document; the equivalence claim is inherited, and I hold it provisionally.

**8.** *"Any other aspects… should be properly reported"* is a new claim, not the checklist's. The checklist says what must appear; this says whatever appears must be accurate and complete. Its analogue is the abstract rule — reflect the article, include nothing absent from the body. It is an accuracy clause, and by construction it cannot enforce completeness, so it cannot swallow the checklist's job unless no item governs a domain people routinely report. Test: take a frequently mentioned, item-less domain — cost-effectiveness is the document's own example — and count "mentioned but inadequately reported" elements per trial over time. Flat or worsening means the clause is inert and an item belongs there. Note that harms were not left to this clause; they were handed to a separate extension.

*Swapping designs.* Crossover breaks item 12a's independence assumption — one observation per participant — through within-participant correlation, carry-over, and period effects; item 6's single pre-specified time point of primary interest also strains. Cluster breaks the unit of randomisation versus analysis: item 3a already asks for the unit ("patient, GP practice, lesion"), item 7a states the sample-size elements "will differ for cluster trials," and the independence clause applies within clusters.

The reason for the limit sits in item 3a's explanation: "The CONSORT statement focuses mainly on trials with participants individually randomised to one of two 'parallel' groups. In fact, little more than half of published trials have such a design." I'd concede "little more than half" is a thin margin for anchoring there — the justification is that it is modal and simplest, not near-universal.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

9. Sort the parts by where they came from. Which of them were worked out with the thing itself in view and could be caught out by a change nobody has tried — allocation concealment, the blinding terminology, the revised item 16 — and which are inherited or asserted: the equivalence of minimisation, the claim that "most of CONSORT is also relevant" to other designs, and the criterion that items are included because they relate to internal and external validity? On that last one: the test for inclusion is "related to validity," and validity in a report is judged from the items. Can I believe the criterion without already believing the checklist, or is the conclusion sitting in the starting point under another name?

10. For the 2010 revision: if the protocol–publication discrepancy evidence and the selective-outcome-reporting evidence had not grown since 2001, would you still have held the meeting in Canada and added the three items? Name the comparison that would tell "the evidence forced the change" apart from "the group revises roughly every nine years." And if nothing can tell them apart, do you have a second, independent job for the revision, or is the timing the whole of it?
transcript.author:
**9.** *Ground-up, falsifiable by change nobody has tried:* allocation concealment — rests on concealment quality tracking effect-estimate inflation, plus enumerated failure modes (envelope opacity, sequential opening); an untried mechanism would be judged by the same logic. Blinding terminology — rests on 200 "double-blind" trials yielding 18 blinded-group combinations and roughly one in five blinding no relevant party; the fix was naming roles, not new vocabulary. Revised item 16 — rests on the 119-report and 403-trial audits.

*Inherited or asserted:* minimisation equivalence — argued, not measured here. "Most of CONSORT is also relevant" to factorial, cluster, crossover, non-inferiority — asserted; the extensions carry the actual work. And the inclusion criterion.

*Circularity.* I can accept "items relate to validity" without already accepting the checklist, because internal and external validity, and selection, performance, detection, and attrition bias, have sources outside CONSORT — trial logic and meta-epidemiological findings. But that purchase is smaller than it appears: "related to validity" cannot adjudicate *which* items belong; every item contends it relates to validity. So as a justification it does sit in the starting point, renamed. The non-circular test is the one I ran elsewhere: does an item's presence or absence track something measurable — effect estimates, reader classification, coding reliability? Where it tracks nothing, the criterion is decoration.

**10.** No. Strip that evidence and the three additions lose their rationale: item 24 (protocol accessible), 3b (changes to methods), 6b (changes to outcomes) exist because 62% of report–protocol comparisons showed a changed, introduced, or omitted primary outcome, and none of 150 reports mentioned it. The document's connective — "the evidence base… has grown considerably… A meeting was therefore convened" — asserts forcing, not scheduling. Item 16's narrowing flows from the same accumulation, so the revision would be thinner, not empty.

*Distinguishing comparison:* map every new or changed item to the studies it cites, by date. If all changes lean on post-2001 work, evidence forced them. If changes cite pre-2001 evidence the group previously declined to act on, the cycle explains them. 1996 to 2001 is five years, 2001 to 2010 is nine — irregular, which weakens a fixed clock, though "when enough accumulated" survives.

*Second job:* yes — clarity, better examples, updated references, glossary moved to the website. Maintenance is independent of new evidence, but it cannot motivate three new items. For those, evidence is the whole of it.

transcript.reader:
Two last ones.

11. If you are right that these items must be reported, what else has to be so that you have not looked at? Take not a reader appraising one trial but a systematic reviewer extracting data, or someone trying to reproduce the intervention from the report. Name one thing that must hold if your explanation is right, tell me whether the checklist does it as it stands or would need a new part, and say which rival version of your explanation that new job rules out.

12. Flip it: suppose reporting became complete and transparent, and effect estimates still tracked how well a trial was run. Which parts of your explanation would have to be different, and which would stay as they are? Then a cut: name the one item where you cannot find any change in the world that would tell it from its nearest neighbour, and say what you would need to see to keep it on the list.
transcript.author:
**11.** The downstream jobs impose a requirement I never stated: the publication must be a sufficient, retrievable proxy for the trial record — item-level information extractable by two independent coders to the same result, and the protocol and registry entry recoverable, dated, and version-stable. For a systematic reviewer that means identical denominators and outcome definitions across article, protocol, and registry. For someone reproducing the intervention, item 5's "sufficient detail" plus the non-pharmacological extension's requirements on expertise and standardisation.

Does the checklist as it stands do it? Partly. Item 24 asks only *where* the protocol can be accessed — a pointer, not an archived document — and nothing requires the registry entry to match the article. So it needs a new part: registration number and date, protocol version, and amendments. What that rules out is the reader-centred account, in which CONSORT exists so an individual clinician can judge validity and relevance. A prose-perfect report whose protocol is unfindable or silently amended satisfies that account completely and still cannot be extracted reproducibly or replicated. Extractability demands record linkage; readability does not. That rival was plausible until you ask what a reviewer, not a reader, has to do.

**12.** *Changes.* My empirical anchor. Where I write that trials not describing X had larger effects, I cannot separate report wording from conduct — unclear reporting is itself a proxy for poor conduct. Under the flip those studies license nothing about reporting. My implicit hope that improving reporting improves estimates goes. So does "reporting is the modifiable proximal target."

*Stays.* The appraisal claim, strengthened: with conduct fixed and reported, the report is the only window onto it. And "CONSORT was not meant to be used as a quality assessment instrument" — now demonstrably, since reporting and conduct vary independently. What shifts is CONSORT's job: from intervention to disclosure. Its function becomes making flawed conduct visible so such trials can be identified and excluded, not preventing bias. "Facilitates critical appraisal" and "improves quality of reporting" survive; anything implying that better reporting yields less bias dies.

*The cut.* Item 2b, specific objectives or hypotheses. The document concedes "objectives and hypotheses are not always easily differentiated," and asserts most reports handle them adequately — an assertion I cannot support. I find no observation separating a stated objective from a stated hypothesis. To keep it I'd need coders distinguishing them above chance with agreement statistics, and evidence that trials with directional hypotheses show fewer protocol–publication outcome discrepancies. Otherwise fold 2b into 2a.

report:
# Hard-to-vary report: CONSORT 2010 Explanation and Elaboration

**1. The question, frozen.** The document answers several. The one its title and opening make central is the reporting claim, as its author narrowed it: *why must a report of a two-group parallel RCT contain each CONSORT item — what does each item let a reader do, and what does its absence cost?* Range: primary reports of individually randomised parallel trials; other designs by published extension. Two further questions were frozen separately when tested: why the 2010 revision was warranted, and whether introducing CONSORT improved reports. Kind: "does this rule do what it is for," backed by backward evidence ("what can we tell from what we see").

**2. The explanation in parts.** (1) The warrant: reporting is measurably incomplete and sometimes inaccurate. (2) Four bias-linked features: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, selective outcome reporting. (3) The remaining items, held by appraisability. (4) Mechanisms: randomisation, concealment, blinding, description-before-analysis. (5) An accuracy clause. (6) Scope limits. (7) The revision history and three new items. (8) The adoption claim. (9) Examples and boxes.

**3. Part by part.** One mark each; no adding up.

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| 1 Warrant | **Held** — by the audits (21%/34% sequence generation, 45%/53% primary outcome, 13% of 119 ITT claims wrong). The percentages are **borrowed** from the named reviews |
| 2 Four bias-linked features | **Held** — concealment adequacy tracks larger estimates; 18 blinded-group combinations in 200 "double blind" trials; 62% of protocol comparisons changed a primary outcome, none of 150 mentioned it |
| 3 Appraisal-only items (2a, 3a, 4a, 4b, 14a, 15) | **Held if** — held by "a reader cannot judge without it," which the author concedes is untested; his gauge: does the item's presence track reader judgment or effect estimates |
| 4 Randomisation's mechanism | **Held** — swap the software package or the seed: nothing moves; drop the random element: it does. The held part is unpredictability, not equal groups |
| 5 Concealment kept apart from blinding | **Held** — swapping them fails: concealment acts before allocation on selection bias, blinding after it on performance and detection bias |
| 6 "Double blind" replaced by named roles | **Held** — by the terminology evidence; the remedy is naming who was blinded |
| 7 Revised item 16 | **Held** — forced by the 119-report and 403-trial audits; declared a new claim, with the old range recorded |
| 8 Sample-size item 7a | **Held** (by "readers can see the size attained"); the debate over whether underpowered trials are permissible is **idle** — the document calls it immaterial to reporting |
| 9 History; new items 24, 3b, 6b | **Held if** — items held by the discrepancy evidence; the timing held by nothing yet, while the "nine-year cycle" rival lives |
| 10 Scope limits | **Fixed** — set by the owners, untested; the stated reason for the design limit ("little more than half of trials") is conceded as thin. Stated openly, so not a silent narrowing |
| 11 Accuracy clause ("any other aspects… reported") | **Loose** — a patch with no gauge until the author supplied one (count mentioned-but-poorly-reported elements over time in an item-free domain, e.g. cost-effectiveness) |
| 12 "Introduction of CONSORT… associated with improved quality" | **Unknown** — no study attached; nearest figures are cross-sectional (70% v 48% for ITT), confounded by journal selection. Test: matched adopting and non-adopting journals, same years |
| 13 Examples; boxes 1–6 | **Held** — by the given job (show what good reporting looks like); the harms item is **borrowed** from the harms extension |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Jobs, and where they came from.* The central job is **given** (the abstract). The bias job is given, but its evidence is borrowed from other people's meta-epidemiology. An **added** job — a systematic reviewer must extract identical denominators, outcomes and dates from article, protocol and registry — was accepted, and it demands a new part (registration number and date, protocol version, amendments). It kills the "CONSORT exists so one clinician can judge validity" rival; the author said so.
*Change list.* Covered: unpredictable versus deterministic sequence; concealed versus unconcealed; blinded versus unblinded assessors; subjective versus objective outcome; single versus multicentre; protocol versus publication; parallel versus other designs. Left out, openly: whether a report is honest or a trial well run — the document separates reporting from conduct.
*Flip.* Complete reporting with conduct still varying kills the bias half (report wording cannot be separated from conduct) and strengthens the appraisal half; the author moved CONSORT's job from preventing bias to making poor conduct visible. Nothing would have been false had the opposite held — so the bias claim is testable only where conduct is measured separately.
*Direction.* Mostly forward (method → estimate), which is right; the adoption sentence runs backwards from "better reports where adopted" and cannot be poked.
*Answer in the starting points.* The inclusion criterion "relates to validity" is the conclusion renamed — conceded; the non-circular substitute is the tracking gauge.
*Pairs that pull.* Balance versus unpredictability: unpredictability gives way, and the price is paid in disclosure (8b requires block size). Minimisation versus the guarantee against unknown factors: the guarantee gives way, on argument, not measurement. Completeness versus word limits: the line is handed to journals, openly.
*Catch-alls.* The accuracy clause, gauge above. By contrast, harms were not left to it but handed to an extension — good practice on the document's own terms.
*Where the parts came from.* Built: concealment, blinding roles, revised item 16, and the removal of the blinding test — a part cut because the measurement could not tell broken blinding from accurate inference, the document applying this method to itself. Fitted: the percentages, and wording tuned across 1996, 2001, 2010. Asserted or inherited: minimisation equivalence, "most of CONSORT is relevant" to other designs, the adoption sentence, the history.
*The cut.* Item 2b (objectives or hypotheses): no observation separates a stated objective from a stated hypothesis. To keep it, the author named agreement statistics and a link to fewer protocol–publication discrepancies; otherwise it folds into 2a.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Three moves, all the author's own. First, run the gauge on each appraisal-only item: does its presence vary with reader classification, coding reliability, or effect estimates adjusted for overall care quality? Flat means it is ornamental, or belongs with the bias items. Second, date-map every new or changed item to the studies it cites; if all lean on post-2001 work the cycle rival dies, if some cite earlier work it survives. Third, attach a study and a comparison to the adoption sentence, or cut its causal reading.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. Most of the document is normative — what a report should contain — and no observation confirms a "should". The tight parts are about the world (concealment, blinding, outcome reporting); much of the remainder is held by "a reader cannot appraise without it", which is close to analytic. This tested a rule's rationale, not whether the rule helps.

**7. One next step.** Run the first gauge on items 4a and 4b: take trials whose protocols hold eligibility and setting detail, and ask whether readers' applicability judgments, or effect estimates, move with how fully those items were reported. If they do not, an item goes or the inclusion criterion is decoration.
